units.t: Wild Nature Shorts. Episode two.
In this episode: The wolves of Yellowstone and Animals that cheat ageing.
Part one. The wolves of Yellowstone.
When wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, they became the centre of one of ecology's most famous stories.
The truth is messier, and more interesting.
Keystone species.
In the 1960s American ecologist Robert Paine ran a simple experiment on the rocky shore of Washington State.
He repeatedly removed a predatory sea star from one stretch of rocks and left a neighbouring stretch alone.
Without the sea star, mussels took over, crowding out other species, and the shore's diversity collapsed.
Paine called such a species a keystone, after the stone at the top of an arch that holds the rest in place.
The idea that predators can shape whole ecosystems through a chain of effects called a trophic cascade became hugely influential.
Sea otters, for instance, protect kelp forests by eating sea urchins.
Wolves in Yellowstone became the most famous test case of all.
Lost and returned.
Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the world's first national park, but early managers saw wolves as vermin that killed livestock and the elk and deer visitors liked to see.
Government hunters shot, trapped and poisoned them, and by the mid-1920s they were gone.
Elk numbers rose, and managers worried about heavy browsing of young aspen, willow and cottonwood.
Rangers at times culled elk themselves.
Attitudes changed, and after the wolf was listed as endangered, plans to restore it gained momentum despite fierce opposition from ranchers.
In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves from Canada were released into the park, and more went to central Idaho.
They thrived, settling at roughly one hundred inside the park, and became a major attraction in the Lamar Valley.
The famous story.
As the wolves settled in, elk numbers on the northern range fell sharply, from around 19,000 in the mid-1990s to a fraction of that within two decades.
Some researchers reported willows and aspens growing taller in places, and beaver colonies increased.
A powerful story took shape.
Wolves, it was said, not only ate elk but frightened them away from exposed valleys and riverbanks, creating a landscape of fear.
Freed from browsing, trees recovered, beavers returned, songbirds followed and riverbanks stabilised.
A short online video in 2014, How Wolves Change Rivers, spread this story to many millions of viewers.
It is a beautiful narrative of nature healing itself, and parts of it are supported by real evidence.
What scientists argue about.
Many ecologists think the popular story is too tidy.
Elk declined for several reasons at once, including predation by cougars and bears as well as wolves, hunting outside the park and drought.
Some studies found elk did not avoid risky places as strongly as the landscape of fear idea suggested, and that aspen often failed to recover even where wolves were common.
Other work found willow recovery was patchy and modest.
One reason is that when beavers vanished, their dams collapsed, streams cut deeper channels and the water table dropped.
Willows on those drier banks struggle however few elk there are.
Researchers still disagree on how much of Yellowstone's change can truly be credited to wolves.
Lessons from the debate.
Decades of radio-collar data make Yellowstone's wolves among the most studied large predators on Earth.
Some effects are well established.
Their kills feed ravens, eagles, magpies, bears and coyotes through winter, and wolves have reshaped the behaviour and numbers of other predators.
Elk herds are smaller and behave differently.
What remains contested is how far those changes flowed down to trees, rivers and the wider landscape.
The debate is not a failure of science but science working, as researchers test an appealing idea against messy data.
The broader lesson is valuable.
Removing a top predator can change an ecosystem for a century, and putting it back does not simply rewind the clock.
The key idea: Some species have effects on their ecosystem far larger than their numbers suggest.
Part two. Animals that cheat ageing.
A shark born before Captain Cook sailed, a rodent that barely seems to age, a jellyfish that turns back its own clock: what nature's longest lives reveal about growing old.
Ming the clam.
In 2006, scientists dredging the seabed off Iceland pulled up an ordinary-looking clam.
It was frozen on board as routine, so it was already dead when researchers counted the growth rings in its shell, much like tree rings, and realised it was extraordinary.
The ocean quahog, nicknamed Ming, was about 507 years old, alive since around the start of the 1500s.
Ming is one of the oldest individual animals whose age has been reliably measured.
Its story raises a big question: if some animals live for centuries, why do others, including us, age and die on a much shorter schedule?
Why do we age.
Ageing is an evolutionary puzzle.
Why would natural selection allow bodies to wear out?
Biologists such as Peter Medawar and George Williams developed an influential answer.
In the wild, most animals die young from predators, disease, accidents or starvation.
Genes that cause problems late in life are rarely 'seen' by natural selection, because few individuals live long enough for them to matter.
Some genes that help early, for example by boosting reproduction, might even cause harm later.
A related idea, the 'disposable soma' theory, says bodies invest in reproduction rather than perfect long-term repair.
It predicts that animals facing less outside danger should age more slowly.
Many long-lived species fit that pattern.
Giants and mole-rats.
The Greenland shark lives in cold North Atlantic and Arctic waters.
Sharks lack bony growth rings, so in 2016 researchers used radiocarbon dating on eye lenses, which form before birth and do not change.
They estimated the largest shark was around 400 years old, with a wide margin of uncertainty, making it the longest-lived vertebrate known.
Bowhead whales may live more than 200 years, and old harpoon tips from the 1800s have been found in whales caught in modern times.
The pink, almost hairless naked mole-rat of East Africa has lived over 30 years in captivity, where a mouse lives two or three.
A study found its risk of dying did not seem to rise with age, unlike almost every other mammal.
It also very rarely gets cancer.
Turning back the clock.
A tiny jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, is nicknamed the immortal jellyfish.
When injured, stressed or old, it can transform back into an earlier life stage, a polyp attached to the seabed, and grow into a new jellyfish.
In principle, it could repeat this many times.
In practice, individuals still die from predators and disease, so it is not truly immortal.
The freshwater hydra, a small relative of jellyfish, also appears to show little or no ageing.
Stem cells constantly renew its body, and in laboratory studies hydra did not show the usual rise in death rate over time.
These animals suggest ageing is not an unbreakable law of biology.
Cancer and our own lives.
Cancer starts when a cell picks up harmful mutations and divides out of control.
So animals with more cells, living longer, should get more cancer.
Yet large animals do not seem to have higher rates than small ones, a puzzle called Peto's paradox.
Elephants have around 20 copies of the TP53 gene, which helps trigger the death of damaged cells, while humans have one pair.
Bowhead whales appear unusually good at repairing DNA.
These animals give researchers real leads.
But they do not yet translate into treatments that extend human life, and many anti-ageing products lack good evidence.
This is general information, not health advice.
The well-tested basics, such as not smoking, staying active, sleeping well and eating well, remain best supported.
The key idea: Some animals live for centuries, and their ages can be read from growth layers, raising the question of why ageing happens at all.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is a keystone species?
Answer. One with outsized effects for its numbers.
Question two. How was the age of Ming the clam worked out?
Answer. Counting growth rings in its shell.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
